"At the end of the nineteenth century, attitudes among Croats and Serbs toward the Habsburg monarchy—formally the Dual Monarchy of Austria-Hungary after the Compromise of 1867—were deeply divided and cannot be reduced to simple loyalty or rebellion. Sentiments differed by region, social class, political party, and generation, and they evolved considerably over the final decades of the century. Croats lived under two halves of the monarchy: Croatia-Slavonia belonged to the Hungarian crown, while Dalmatia and Istria were administered from Vienna. Serbs were even more dispersed, with large communities in Croatia-Slavonia, Dalmatia, and southern Hungary, an occupied Bosnia-Herzegovina after 1878, and, of course, an independent Serbian kingdom outside the empire altogether.

Among Croats, the 1860s had been marked by Austro-Slavism—the hope that Vienna would champion the Slavs against German and Hungarian centralism. Bishop Josip Juraj Strossmayer embodied this current, promoting the idea of Yugoslav cultural unity and financing the Yugoslav Academy and the University of Zagreb, while quietly hoping for a trialist reorganization of the empire that would create a third, South Slavic unit alongside Austria and Hungary. The Croatian-Hungarian Settlement of 1868, however, disappointed these hopes. It confirmed Hungarian supremacy over Croatia in matters of finance, trade, and railways, and many Croats came to see the dualist structure as fundamentally unjust: the Hungarians had their historical state rights recognized, while Croatian autonomy was reduced to a hollow formality.

This frustration deepened dramatically during the long banate of Károly Khuen-Héderváry (1883–1903), whose aggressive Magyarization—imposing Hungarian in administration, schools, and public symbolism—provoked mounting resentment. A telling episode came in October 1895, when Emperor Francis Joseph visited Zagreb: a group of Croatian university students publicly burned the Hungarian flag in protest. The university was temporarily closed and the students expelled, an event that radicalized an entire generation. Significantly, however, the anger was directed chiefly at Budapest rather than at the emperor himself; many Croats still regarded the monarch as a potential arbiter against Hungarian oppression, and rumors that the heir Franz Ferdinand favored trialism kept faint hopes alive.

Croatian political currents reflected this ambivalence. The conservative Catholic establishment, the bureaucracy, and much of the officer corps remained genuinely loyal to the dynasty, which they saw as a shield against Italian irredentism in Dalmatia and, increasingly, against Serbian and Orthodox expansion. The official jubilee celebrations of Francis Joseph in 1898 revealed this loyalist current, even as opposition circles used the occasion to demonstrate against the regime. By contrast, Ante Starčević's Party of Right preached the Croatian 'state right' and in principle rejected Habsburg rule altogether; its radical wing had risen in armed revolt at Rakovica as early as 1871. Yet even Starčević softened toward Vienna in the 1880s, fearing Serbia and Russia more than the emperor, and a faction of the party cooperated opportunistically with Khuen's government in the Sabor. Ordinary peasants, squeezed economically and affected by Magyarization of local life, added a reservoir of latent discontent that opposition politicians increasingly drew upon.

Serbian sentiments were even more layered. Within the monarchy, the Serbs carried a long historical memory of privileged loyalty: their church at Karlovci, their settlements in the former Military Frontier, and their service to the dynasty against Hungary in 1848–49 bound many, especially older elites and clergy, to Vienna. But grievances accumulated steadily. The abolition of the Military Frontier in 1881 removed a cherished institutional status; Hungarian language and education laws of the late 1870s and 1880s pressured Serbian schools in Vojvodina; and the trial and imprisonment of the national leader Svetozar Miletić in the early 1880s made him a martyr and radicalized Serbian opinion. Khuen's strategy of favoring Serbian deputies in Croatia in order to play them against the Croats won some short-term loyalty but ultimately embittered both communities. By the late 1890s, a notable rapprochement was underway—symbolized by the 1897 agreement between Starčević and Miletić's followers—which would culminate after 1905 in the joint Croat-Serb coalition politics of the 'new course.'

Serbia proper presented a different picture. Officially, the kingdom of Milan Obrenović and then Alexander was tied to Vienna: a secret convention of 1881 bound Serbia to follow Austria-Hungary's lead in the Balkans in exchange for dynastic support, and Serbia's economy was locked into the Habsburg market through its exports of livestock. Public opinion, however, was far less compliant. The Congress of Berlin in 1878, which placed Bosnia-Herzegovina under Austro-Hungarian occupation, was widely experienced in Serbia as a betrayal of their Orthodox brethren; the fierce Bosnian resistance of 1878 and the crushing of the uprising left lasting bitterness. The humiliating war with Bulgaria in 1885, and Vienna's role in ending it, further wounded national pride. The People's Radical Party under Nikola Pašić, drawing on peasants and the nationalist intelligentsia, leaned toward Russia and against Habsburg tutelage, so that even in the 1890s—before the dramatic rupture after 1903—one could already sense the tension between Serbia's economic dependence on the monarchy and its growing political-national resentment of it.

Bosnia-Herzegovina deserves mention as well: both its Serbian and Croatian populations largely resented the occupation, and Croatian nationalists considered the province part of the Croatian lands by state right, while Serbian nationalists saw it as the heart of the Serbian question. Thus the monarchy's presence in the Balkans created grievances that resonated on both sides of the border.

In sum, at the close of the nineteenth century Croatian and Serbian attitudes toward the Habsburg monarchy ranged from sincere dynastic loyalty among conservatives, officials, and the Catholic and Orthodox hierarchies, through pragmatic cooperation by opportunistic party leaders, to fierce opposition rooted in national rights, resentment of Hungarian dominance, and the dream of South Slavic unity. The dominant trajectory across the 1890s was one of growing alienation: hopes invested in trialism and imperial arbitration were fading, hostility was shifting from Budapest alone toward the entire dualist order, and Croat-Serb cooperation against common grievances was emerging. The feelings were thus conditional rather than absolute—loyal in form, frustrated in substance—setting the stage for the crises of the early twentieth century."

Part 1. Task Summary

Implement a distributed rate limiting service for the public REST API gateway.

**Scope:**
- Build a token-bucket rate limiter enforced at the API gateway layer, backed by Redis for distributed, cross-instance state.
- Support per-API-key limits with configurable tiers (Free: 60 req/min, Pro: 600 req/min, Enterprise: custom).
- Return standard rate limit headers (`X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, `X-RateLimit-Reset`, `Retry-After`) on all responses, including 429s.
- Expose an internal admin endpoint for viewing and adjusting per-key limits.
- Roll out in shadow (log-only) mode before enforcing rejections.

**Out of scope:**
- Billing integration for overage charges (tracked separately, see TODO-421).
- Rate limiting for WebSocket/gRPC traffic.
- A customer-facing self-serve limits dashboard (planned for a future cycle).

**Key deliverables:** `rate-limiter` Go library (v1.0.0), gateway integration in `edge-gateway`, Redis Lua scripts for atomic bucket operations, Grafana dashboard + alerts, and developer docs.

***

Part 2. Motivation

- **Incident-driven need.** On 2025-11-03 and 2025-11-19, runaway customer scripts saturated the product search endpoint, causing p99 latency to exceed 4s for all tenants and triggering two customer-visible outages (INC-1187, INC-1203). We currently have no mechanism to contain a single tenant's load.
- **Fair usage.** Without per-tenant limits, heavy users degrade service quality for everyone. Rate limiting provides predictable, equitable access.
- **Commercial requirements.** The new tiered pricing plan (launching Q1, per Sales/PM) requires differentiated API limits as a paid feature. This work is a blocking dependency for that launch.
- **Support burden.** Support receives ~15 tickets/month related to API abuse and accidental hammering by customer integrations. Headers and `Retry-After` guidance will let customers self-correct without contacting support.
- **Security.** Limits reduce the blast radius of credential-stuffing and scraping attempts against the public API.

***

Part 3. Milestone objectives

**M1 — Design approved**
- Finalize algorithm choice (token bucket with burst capacity = 2x sustained rate).
- Approve Redis key schema and TTL strategy; review atomicity guarantees of Lua scripts.
- Agree on header spec and 429 response body format with API governance.
- *Exit criteria:* RFC reviewed and signed off by gateway, platform, and API governance teams.

**M2 — Core library**
- `rate-limiter` Go package implementing token bucket against Redis (Lua script for atomic check-and-decrement).
- Fail-open behavior on Redis unavailability (with alerting), configurable per environment.
- Unit and integration test coverage ≥ 85%, including race/atomicity tests against a real Redis instance.
- *Exit criteria:* Library published to internal registry as v1.0.0 and adopted by at least one non-gateway service in shadow mode.

**M3 — Gateway integration**
- `edge-gateway` middleware resolves API key → tier → limit, evaluates request, and attaches response headers.
- Admin endpoint (internal-only) to read/update per-key overrides; changes propagate in < 30s.
- Load test at 2x projected peak traffic with no added p99 latency beyond 5ms.
- *Exit criteria:* Middleware merged behind a feature flag, defaulting to shadow mode in all environments.

**M4 — Observability**
- Metrics: allowed/rejected counts by tier and key, Redis latency, fail-open events.
- Grafana dashboard and PagerDuty alert on fail-open rate > 0.1% for 5 minutes.
- *Exit criteria:* Dashboard live in production; on-call runbook updated and reviewed.

**M5 — Rollout and docs**
- Two weeks in shadow mode to validate rejection rates against real traffic; tune tier thresholds with PM sign-off.
- Staged enforcement: 1% → 10% → 50% → 100% of traffic, at least 48 hours per stage.
- Developer docs published: limits by tier, header semantics, retry/backoff guidance; changelog announcement sent to API consumers.
- *Exit criteria:* Enforcement at 100% with rejection error rate < 0.5% of total requests and no open sev-2+ issues for one week.

# The Reality of Disability: What We Get Wrong, and What Has to Change

Disability is one of the most common human experiences on Earth — and one of the least honestly discussed. The World Health Organization estimates that roughly 1.3 billion people, about one in six worldwide, live with significant disability. In the United States, the CDC reports that one in four adults has one. Add in family members, partners, and friends, and disability touches virtually every household. Yet public conversation still tends to treat it as rare, tragic, and someone else's problem.

It's time to talk about what the reality actually looks like.

## More Than a Medical Diagnosis

For decades, disability was understood through what researchers call the *medical model*: a personal misfortune to be treated, fixed, or pitied. Disabled activists and scholars have pushed back with a different framing — the *social model* — which holds that people are often disabled less by their bodies than by their environments.

A wheelchair user isn't disabled by their legs; they're disabled by the stairs. A Deaf person isn't disabled by their ears; they're disabled by a meeting with no interpreter or captions. A neurodivergent employee isn't disabled by their brain; they're disabled by rigid systems designed for one kind of mind. This shift matters because it changes the solution: instead of asking disabled people to adapt to the world, it asks the world to adapt.

## The Economics of Being Disabled

The financial reality is stark. Disabled adults face unemployment rates roughly twice those of non-disabled adults — not because of capability, but because of inflexible workplaces, biased hiring, and inaccessible infrastructure. Those who do work are often paid less and promoted less.

Then there are the extra costs that non-disabled people never think about: wheelchairs and hearing aids not covered by insurance, accessible housing that commands a premium, specialized transportation, medications, therapies, and home modifications. Research consistently finds that disabled people need roughly a quarter to a third more income just to achieve the same standard of living as everyone else. In many countries, the benefits system makes this worse, clawing back support the moment a person tries to save money or work part-time — trapping people in poverty by design.

## The Burden of Proof

Most disabilities are invisible: chronic pain, autoimmune disease, psychiatric conditions, learning disabilities, hearing loss, long COVID. People with these conditions face a peculiar cruelty — the constant suspicion of faking it.

They're confronted in parking lots for using accessible spaces. They're told "but you don't *look* sick." They must document, prove, and re-prove their limitations to employers, insurers, and agencies year after year. Many describe "spoon theory" — the practice of budgeting a limited daily supply of energy — while also spending some of those precious spoons just convincing others that the budget exists.

## Inspiration Is Not Equality

The late activist Stella Young coined a term for a familiar genre: *inspiration porn*. It's the viral video of a disabled person doing something ordinary — shopping, dancing, graduating — framed as extraordinary simply because they're disabled. It feels uplifting, but it carries a hidden message: that disability itself is a tragedy, and that a disabled person's greatest achievement is existing at all.

The reality is far more human. Disabled people have jobs, businesses, relationships, hobbies, and strong opinions. They laugh, get annoyed, travel, parent, and binge terrible television. They are not here to be inspirations. They are here to be people.

## Progress — and the Distance Left to Go

Real gains have been made. The Americans with Disabilities Act (1990) and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (2006) established legal foundations for access and equality. Curb cuts, captions, screen readers, and remote work have changed millions of lives — and improved life for everyone else, too.

But enforcement is patchy. Digital platforms remain riddled with barriers. Disabled people — especially disabled women and disabled people of color — face higher rates of poverty, abuse, and exclusion from healthcare. And in too many boardrooms, legislatures, and design studios, decisions about disabled people are still made without them.

## Where Change Begins

The disability community has a saying: *nothing about us without us*. It's both a demand and a roadmap. Accessibility should be designed in from the start, not bolted on as an afterthought. Disabled people belong in leadership, media, medicine, and government — not merely as subjects of policy, but as its authors.

For individuals, the path is simpler than it seems: believe people about their own bodies. Ask, don't assume. Support accessibility even when it doesn't affect you. And stop mistaking pity for compassion — the first looks down, while the second builds a world where looking down is never necessary.

The reality of disability is not a story of limitation. It is a story of barriers — most of them human-made, which means most of them can be unmade. If this article leaves you with questions — about accessibility, language, or how to be a genuine ally — then the conversation is exactly where it should be. Keep asking.

This quote is often attributed to Albert Einstein though there is no solid evidence that he ever said it. The line actually appears in a novel by Rita Mae Brown from the early 1990s. The misattribution is itself revealing because people want their aphorisms blessed by genius. A clever saying about God gains weight when we imagine it falling from the mouth of the greatest scientist of the modern age. The irony runs deep because Einstein professed belief in a God of order and natural law rather than a personal deity who arranges meetings and missed trains.

What does the quote actually claim? It suggests that the strange alignments of life are not random at all. When you bump into an old friend on a street corner in a foreign city and that meeting changes the direction of your career the quote whispers that someone planned this. God wanted to help you but did not want to sign his name. The miracle is real yet the evidence is missing. Faith fills the gap.

I think the quote succeeds first as literature. Great aphorisms take two ideas that seem unrelated and weld them together with a shock of recognition. Coincidence is normally the enemy of meaning. It is what we say when no better explanation exists. Yet the quote flips this. It turns the absence of explanation into a signature of presence. That reversal is genuinely witty. It is the kind of line that makes you pause before you laugh.

There is also a long theological tradition behind it. Christian thinkers have spoken of providence which is the belief that God governs the world through ordinary means rather than through constant miracles. Luther wrote about the hidden God. Pascal suggested that there is enough light for those who seek and enough shadow for those who do not care. The quote compresses that entire tradition into one playful sentence. It says that the divine prefers subtlety to spectacle. An anonymous God leaves room for doubt because forced belief would mean nothing. Love that is compelled is not love at all. Perhaps the same logic applies to faith.

The psychological reading is just as interesting. Human beings are pattern seeking animals. We find faces in clouds and hear messages in static and draw meaning from chance overlaps. We also suffer from confirmation bias which means we remember the times a hunch paid off and forget the countless times it did not. The quote can be read as a poetic description of this mental machinery. Perhaps we call coincidence an anonymous God because our minds are built to crave authorship. A story with no author feels intolerable. We would rather have a hidden author than no author at all.

A skeptic would press on the fact that the claim is unfalsifiable. If every chance event might be divine then nothing can ever count against the belief. No experiment could be devised and no evidence gathered. Some see this as a fatal flaw. Others see it as the whole point of faith which by definition trusts beyond the reach of proof. The quote sits exactly on that fault line and refuses to resolve it. That refusal is part of its charm and part of its danger.

For believers the line offers real comfort. It lets them live inside a scientific worldview without feeling that science has emptied the world of wonder. Rain has a meteorological explanation yet the timing of the rain on the day of the wedding can still feel like a gift. The quote gives people permission to read grace into the gaps without abandoning reason entirely. It is a treaty between belief and explanation.

There is a caution worth adding. This style of thinking can slide into magical thinking. If every coincidence carries a message then we may start reading meaning into pure noise. We might make major decisions based on parking spots and overheard conversations. We might also use the idea to soften events that deserve our honest grief. Not every loss is a blessing in disguise. Some tragedies are simply tragic and dressing them up as secret providence can become a way of avoiding pain rather than facing it.

Carl Jung noticed something similar with his idea of synchronicity. He described meaningful coincidences that resist explanation by cause and effect. Jung thought these events pointed to some deep pattern in the psyche and the world alike. Scientists remain skeptical of his framework. Still his intuition overlaps with the spirit of the quote. Both suggest that meaning might be woven into reality rather than projected onto it. Both also admit that we cannot prove it.

What I find most compelling about the line is what it reveals about the human heart rather than about God. It endures because it captures a tension that everyone feels. We know the universe runs on probability and yet our lives keep presenting us with moments that feel curated. Maybe those moments are statistical illusions. Maybe they are providence. Maybe they are both in some way we cannot articulate. The quote does not resolve the question. It simply names the question with unusual elegance.

In the end I would say this. Whether or not anyone is hiding behind the curtain of chance the way we interpret randomness shapes how we live. People who see anonymous grace tend to move through the world with gratitude. People who see only chance tend to move through it with curiosity. Perhaps the healthiest stance holds both dispositions at once. Stay open to wonder while staying honest about uncertainty. The quote asks us to do exactly that. It invites belief without demanding it and it leaves the signature page blank on purpose.

# Lecture Outline: *La La Land* (2016) — Dreaming in Cinemascope

**Duration:** ~60–75 minutes
**Note:** This outline assumes students have watched the film beforehand. Consider opening with a brief clip if they haven't.

---

## I. Opening Hook (5 minutes)

- **Engagement activity:** Play "Another Day of Sun" as students enter the room.
- **Discussion prompt:** "What does it cost to chase a dream?" Have students jot down a one-sentence answer to revisit at the end of class.
- Briefly mention the infamous 2017 Oscar Best Picture mix-up with *Moonlight* as an attention-grabbing trivia moment.

## II. Background and Context (10 minutes)

- **Director:** Damien Chazelle — the youngest Best Director Oscar winner (age 32); previously directed *Whiplash* (2014).
- **Cast:** Ryan Gosling (Sebastian) and Emma Stone (Mia); Stone won Best Actress.
- **Production facts:**
  - Shot on 35mm film in Cinemascope (2.55:1 ratio) to evoke classic Hollywood.
  - Gosling learned piano for the role; Stone had no professional dance training.
- **Genre context:** Why did Chazelle revive the classic Hollywood musical? Discuss the genre's decline and its nostalgic place in cinema history (reference influences: *Singin' in the Rain*, *The Umbrellas of Cherbourg*, *An American in Paris*).

## III. Plot Overview (8 minutes)

- Set in Los Angeles: Mia, an aspiring actress working at a coffee shop, and Sebastian, a jazz traditionalist, meet and fall in love.
- The central tension: their individual dreams (acting, owning a jazz club) begin to conflict with their relationship.
- The bittersweet ending — a time-skip epilogue imagining an alternate life together.

## IV. Major Themes (15 minutes)

- **Ambition vs. love:** Can personal dreams coexist with a romantic partnership?
- **Sacrifice and compromise:** The film asks whether success requires losing something essential.
- **Nostalgia vs. modernity:** Sebastian's devotion to "pure" jazz mirrors the film's own love of old Hollywood forms.
- **Dreamers and dreamers' fees:** The recurring question — "Who else is a dreamer here?" — and the film's ambivalent answer about what dreams cost.
- **In-class discussion:** Divide students into small groups, assign each group one theme, and have them find one scene that supports it. Report back.

## V. Cinematic Style and Techniques (12 minutes)

- **Color symbolism:** Mia's shifting dress colors (blue, green, yellow, red) as emotional signposts; the saturated primaries of the musical fantasy sequences vs. muted reality.
- **The opening number ("Another Day of Sun"):** A long, complex single-take on a freeway — a statement of intent about scale and old-school showmanship.
- **The "A Lovely Night" dance sequence:** Discuss the one-take shooting style and its homage to Gene Kelly.
- **The epilogue:** A fantasy montage that reframes the entire film — what does it mean that we see the life they *could* have had?
- **Seasonal chapter titles:** How "Winter," "Spring," "Summer," "Fall" structure the romance like a classic musical.

## VI. The Music (8 minutes)

- Briefly play/analyze key songs:
  - "City of Stars" — Best Original Song winner
  - "Audition (The Fools Who Dream)" — the film's thematic thesis
  - "Mia & Sebastian's Theme" — the leitmotif that recurs and transforms
- **Discussion point:** How does the score bind the film together emotionally?

## VII. Critical Debates (8 minutes)

- Criticism: Is the film's portrayal of jazz problematic (a white character as its "savior")?
- Debate: Is the ending tragic, hopeful, or realistic?
- Question: Does the film romanticize struggle, or honestly depict it?

## VIII. Wrap-Up and Assessment (5–7 minutes)

- Return to the opening question: "What does it cost to chase a dream?" — Have students compare their initial answer to how they'd answer now.
- **Exit ticket:** One paragraph — "Was Mia and Sebastian's decision to part ways justified?"
- **Optional homework:** Write a one-page analysis of a single scene's use of color, music, or camera movement.

---

**Teaching tips:**
- Keep clips short (1–2 minutes each) to maintain pacing.
- The theme group activity and the exit ticket provide two low-stakes chances for every student to speak or write.
- If time allows, a closing "which is better: the dream or the person?" class vote can spark lively debate.

"How to Raise Awareness for a Cause: A Practical Guide

Whether you care deeply about environmental protection, mental health, education, or animal welfare, spreading the word about your cause can feel overwhelming. The good news is that you don't need a huge budget or celebrity connections to make a difference. With a clear strategy and consistent effort, anyone can amplify a message that matters. Here are five practical approaches to raising awareness effectively.

**Section 1: Define Your Message Clearly**

Before you can raise awareness, you need to know exactly what you're raising awareness for. Distill your cause into a single, memorable statement. Instead of a vague goal like "helping the planet," try something specific: "reducing single-use plastic in our local schools." A focused message is easier to remember, easier to share, and easier to act on. Write it down, test it on friends, and refine it until it resonates.

**Section 2: Know Your Audience**

Awareness only matters if it reaches the right people. Ask yourself: who has the power to make a difference, and who is most affected by this issue? A campaign aimed at lawmakers will look very different from one aimed at teenagers or local business owners. Research where your audience spends their time, what language they use, and what motivates them. Tailoring your message to your audience dramatically increases your chances of being heard.

**Section 3: Choose the Right Channels**

Different platforms serve different purposes. Social media is ideal for quick updates, visuals, and viral moments. Email newsletters build deeper relationships with supporters over time. Community events, workshops, and local partnerships create face-to-face connections that digital tools can't replicate. Don't try to be everywhere at once—pick two or three channels where your audience is most active and commit to showing up consistently.

**Section 4: Tell Stories, Not Just Statistics**

Facts and figures are important, but stories are what move people to care and act. A single personal narrative—a family affected by the issue, a volunteer's transformative experience, or a community that changed for the better—can be more persuasive than pages of data. Use your statistics to back up your stories, not replace them. When people feel emotionally connected to a cause, they are far more likely to share it with others.

**Section 5: Build Community and Sustain Momentum**

Awareness isn't a one-time event; it's an ongoing effort. Create opportunities for people to get involved, whether that's volunteering, donating, attending events, or simply sharing your content. Celebrate small wins publicly to keep supporters motivated, and give your community a name or identity they can rally around. Consistency builds trust, and trust builds a movement that lasts far longer than any single campaign.

Raising awareness for a cause doesn't happen overnight, but every conversation started, every story shared, and every person informed brings you one step closer to real change. Start small, stay committed, and watch your impact grow."

# Princess Elara and the Dragon of Mount Cinder

Once upon a time, in a kingdom cradled by mountains, there lived a princess named Elara who loved questions more than jewels. While other children of the court practiced curtsies and sword drills, Elara asked why the stars turned and why bees hummed, until the whole palace sighed fondly whenever she entered a room.

One autumn, the river that fed the kingdom ran thin, then trickled, then stopped altogether. The wheat withered in the fields, and the people grew afraid.

"A dragon has settled on Mount Cinder," the watchman announced. "Smoke curls from its peak every night."

Three knights climbed the mountain, one after another, each armed with sword and shield. Each returned singed, soot-blackened, and empty-handed. The king offered half his kingdom to whoever could rid the land of the beast, but no one dared try.

Only Elara packed a different sort of satchel: bread, a jar of honey, a woolen blanket, and her book of riddles.

"You cannot fight a dragon," the king protested.

"I don't mean to fight it," Elara replied. "I mean to ask it a question."

She climbed for two days through wind and scree. On the third morning she found the dragon coiled at the summit, its scales glinting like frozen moonlight, its great amber eyes following her every step.

"Have you come to slay me, like the others?" the dragon rumbled.

"No," Elara replied, setting down her satchel. "I brought bread and honey, because I guessed you must be hungry. And I brought a question: why have you taken our river?"

The dragon was quiet for a long while. Then it uncoiled and shifted aside, revealing a nest of warm black stones—and there, nestled within, lay a single egg as large as a cartwheel.

"The spring runs cold this high up in autumn," the dragon said. "A dragon egg must be kept warm and wet, or it will never hatch. So I blocked the stream and let the water pool here for my little one. I never meant to empty your kingdom. I am sorry."

Elara looked at the egg, then at the shivering mother, then at the first stars appearing overhead. "Then we have a riddle to solve together," she said. "Not how to be rid of a dragon, but how to keep an egg cozy without stealing a river."

They talked until dawn, the princess and the dragon, trading riddles over honeyed bread. At last, Elara clapped her hands. "Hot springs! I've read of them—water warmed by the mountain's own fire. If we dig channels to the nest, the cold stream can run free again."

The dragon flew her home that very morning, which caused rather a stir at the palace gates. With the king's blessing—granted quite quickly once a dragon was politely waiting outside the walls—Elara led a crew of miners and engineers up the mountain. They carved stone channels from the hot springs to the nest, and steaming water curled around the great egg like a warm bath. The cold spring tumbled free down the mountainside, and the river ran strong and silver once more.

In spring, the egg hatched, and the whole kingdom climbed the mountain to celebrate. The mother dragon bowed her enormous head to Elara, and from that day on she guarded the valley, breathing gentle warmth over the fields in winter and turning aside storms with one sweep of her wing.

As for Elara, she never stopped asking questions. But now, every evening, a dragon and her growing daughter would curl around the castle tower to answer them.

And they all lived happily, and curiously, ever after.

Your friend's advice contains a kernel of truth, but it is not the best method for a bike chain. Coke does contain phosphoric acid, which can chemically react with RUST and help loosen it from metal surfaces. However, the soda also contains a lot of sugar, which leaves a sticky residue on your chain if you do not clean it off THOROUGHLY. That residue will attract dirt and grime, which is the last thing you want on a bicycle drivetrain. The Coke method is also slow and messy compared to alternatives that cost about the same.

The STEEL WOOL part of the advice is where things get more questionable. Steel wool is fairly aggressive and can scratch the metal surfaces of your chain. It can also leave behind tiny steel fragments that embed themselves in the links and rollers. Those fragments can promote new rust and accelerate wear over time. A bike chain is a precision component with tight tolerances, so you want to avoid anything too abrasive.

A better approach starts with removing the chain from the bike, if possible, so you can soak it. Soak it first in a degreaser to strip away old oil and grime. For the rust itself, white vinegar or a citric acid solution works better than COKE and leaves far less residue. Let the chain soak for twenty to thirty minutes, then scrub it with a stiff NYLON BRUSH or an old toothbrush. A brass brush is another good option because brass is softer than chain steel and will not gouge it.

After scrubbing, rinse the chain with clean water and dry it completely right away. Any leftover moisture will cause fresh rust to form surprisingly fast. Once the chain is bone dry, apply a quality chain LUBRICANT to every link. This step is essential, not optional, because freshly exposed bare metal is extremely vulnerable to corrosion. Wipe off the excess lube so it does not attract dirt while you ride.

Finally, check whether the chain is worn out, since a chain that has been rusty for a long time may be stretched or structurally compromised. An inexpensive chain checker tool measures this wear for you. If the chain is too worn, replacing it is both safer and more effective than any cleaning method. # The Secret to a Great Night's Sleep: Simple Habits That Actually Work

If you've ever spent an hour tossing and turning, watching the clock tick closer to your alarm, you're not alone. Millions of people struggle to fall asleep or stay asleep, and poor sleep affects everything from our mood to our immune system. The good news? Better sleep doesn't require expensive gadgets or prescription fixes. It starts with a few intentional habits. Here's how to set yourself up for genuinely restful nights.

## Stick to a Consistent Schedule

Your body thrives on routine. Going to bed and waking up at the same time every day—even on weekends—trains your internal clock, making it easier to fall asleep naturally and wake up feeling refreshed. It's tempting to "catch up" on sleep Saturday morning, but those lie-ins can actually throw off your rhythm and make Sunday night miserable. Pick a schedule you can maintain seven days a week, and your body will thank you.

## Create a Sleep-Friendly Environment

Your bedroom should signal one thing to your brain: rest. Keep it cool (around 65°F or 18°C is ideal), dark, and quiet. Blackout curtains, a white noise machine, or a simple fan can make a world of difference. And yes—invest in comfortable bedding. You spend a third of your life in bed, so it's worth it.

## Put the Phone Down

We've all heard it before, but it bears repeating: screens and sleep don't mix. The blue light emitted by phones, tablets, and TVs suppresses melatonin, the hormone that tells your body it's time to wind down. Worse, scrolling through social media or emails keeps your mind stimulated when it should be relaxing. Try powering down at least 30 to 60 minutes before bed. Swap the scroll for a book, gentle stretching, or a few minutes of deep breathing.

## Watch What You Consume

That afternoon coffee is still working its magic at midnight—caffeine can linger in your system for six hours or more. Aim to cut off caffeine by early afternoon, and go easy on alcohol, which may make you drowsy at first but disrupts deep sleep later in the night. Heavy meals close to bedtime can also interfere with rest, so try to finish eating two to three hours before you turn in.

## Build a Wind-Down Ritual

Your body needs a transition period between the busyness of the day and sleep. Create a calming routine that tells your brain it's time to slow down: take a warm shower, dim the lights, journal, or listen to soothing music. Over time, these cues become powerful sleep signals.

## Get Moving—and Get Outside

Regular exercise is one of the best sleep boosters out there, as long as you finish intense workouts a few hours before bed. Just as important is morning light exposure. Natural sunlight early in the day helps regulate your circadian rhythm, making it easier to feel sleepy at night.

## When to Seek Help

If you've tried everything and still struggle to sleep, don't just accept it. Chronic insomnia or persistent daytime fatigue can signal an underlying issue like sleep apnea. Talk to your doctor—help is available, and you deserve real answers.

## The Bottom Line

Great sleep isn't about one magic trick; it's about layering small, consistent habits that work together. Start with one or two changes this week—maybe a consistent bedtime and no phone in bed—and build from there. Your body already knows how to sleep. Your job is simply to get out of its way.

## 1. Executive Summary

This proposal outlines a three-year initiative to improve learning outcomes in under-resourced schools through artificial intelligence. The project will deploy an offline-capable adaptive learning platform along with AI tools that support teachers and identify struggling students early. We plan to pilot the program in three countries and reach fifty thousand learners by the end of year three.

## 2. Background and Problem Statement

Many schools in low-income regions face severe shortages of trained teachers and learning materials. Classrooms often hold fifty or more students with a single instructor. Individualized attention becomes nearly impossible under these conditions. Learners who fall behind rarely receive timely support. Dropout rates rise and foundational skills in literacy and numeracy remain weak. Existing digital education tools usually assume reliable internet and costly devices. That assumption excludes the very communities that need the most help.

## 3. Project Objectives

- Deploy an adaptive learning platform in 200 pilot schools across three countries
- Train 1000 teachers to use AI tools for lesson planning and assessment
- Develop speech and text models for at least five local languages
- Reduce dropout rates through an early warning system
- Demonstrate measurable learning gains of at least 20 percent on standardized assessments

## 4. Proposed Solution

Our solution combines four machine learning components designed for low-resource settings.

**Adaptive Learning Engine**
Students work through lessons on shared tablets. The engine adjusts difficulty in real time based on each response. Models run locally on the device so the platform works without internet access. Progress data syncs whenever connectivity becomes available.

**AI Tutor via Messaging**
Learners can ask questions through WhatsApp or SMS in their own language. A multilingual language model answers with curriculum-aligned explanations. This feature serves students who share devices or study at home.

**Automated Assessment and Feedback**
Machine vision models grade handwritten exercises and give instant feedback. Teachers save hours of marking time each week and can focus on instruction.

**Early Warning System**
A predictive model analyzes attendance and performance data to flag students at risk of dropping out. The system recommends specific interventions for each flagged learner.

## 5. Technology and Infrastructure

- Offline-first Android application built for low-cost tablets
- Lightweight models that run on inexpensive hardware
- Solar charging kits for schools with unreliable electricity
- Local data storage to protect student privacy
- Open-source base models fine-tuned on national curricula

## 6. Language and Inclusion

We will partner with local universities to collect speech and text data in underrepresented languages. Fine-tuned models will support oral learning traditions common in many regions. The interface will include audio support for early learners and students with low literacy. Gender inclusion targets will ensure that girls have equal access to devices and program benefits.

## 7. Implementation Timeline

**Phase One (Months 1 to 6):** Community needs assessment and stakeholder engagement. Baseline learning data collection in pilot schools.

**Phase Two (Months 7 to 12):** Platform development and pilot launch in 20 schools. Iterative testing with teachers and students.

**Phase Three (Year 2):** Scale to 200 schools. Deliver teacher training workshops. Expand language coverage.

**Phase Four (Year 3):** Full deployment. Independent impact evaluation. Handover planning with ministries of education.

Total request: USD 1.2 million over three years.

- Platform development: 30 percent
- Hardware and connectivity: 25 percent
- Teacher training and support: 20 percent
- Language data collection and localization: 15 percent

The megaliths of Europe take several striking forms. The most iconic is the standing stone, or menhir — a single tall slab planted upright in the ground, appearing alone, in long rows, or in great circles. Stonehenge in England is the most famous example, with massive horizontal lintels balanced atop paired uprights, some rising over twenty feet and weighing many tons. Dolmens are another common type: table-like structures of two or more upright stones supporting an enormous flat capstone, originally often buried within earthen mounds that have since worn away. Passage graves consist of stone chambers and corridors roofed with huge slabs and hidden beneath round mounds, such as Newgrange in Ireland. Most were raised between roughly 6,500 and 3,500 years ago, long before written records existed in the region.

******

In appearance, these ancient monuments are typically grey, rugged, and deeply weathered, often streaked with lichen and moss after millennia in the open air. Builders generally used local rock — granite, sandstone, or limestone — sometimes shaped roughly but usually left natural, giving them a raw, imposing look. Some stand in vast alignments, like the thousands of stones arranged in parallel rows at Carnac in Brittany, France, while others form circles or horseshoes. Chambered tombs appear as low grassy mounds or heaps of smaller stones concealing inner rooms built from giant slabs, and a few, such as Newgrange, bear carved spirals and geometric patterns on their kerbstones. Single stones can be astonishingly large: the Grand Menhir Brisé in Brittany originally stood nearly twenty meters tall before toppling and shattering into pieces that still lie scattered today.

The opposite of youth is not age, but *the loss of wonder*.

Age is simply a number written on the body; it arrives whether we like it or not. A person of seventy can be youthful if they still marvel at sunsets, still ask questions, still believe the best is ahead.

Another possible answer: the opposite of youth is *cynicism*. Youth is defined by its openness — its belief that things can change, that dreams are worth chasing, that failure is just a detour. Cynicism closes those doors. It whispers that nothing really matters, that effort is pointless, that hope is naïve. That is the true ending of youth, not wrinkles or gray hair.

So perhaps the completion of the sentence is this: *we do not grow old by the years we live, but by the curiosity and hope we abandon*. As long as we keep wondering and believing, some part of youth never leaves us.

# The Cat Who Waited

Whiskers had known only one home in his seven years of life. The little gray tabby had been adopted as a kitten by the Morrison family, and he had grown up alongside their two children. Every morning, he would wake young Emma with gentle taps of his paw, and every evening, he would curl up on Mr. Morrison's lap while the family watched television. Life was warm, predictable, and full of love. *He never imagined it could end.*

It happened on a stormy October afternoon. The family piled into their car for what Whiskers assumed was an ordinary trip. But somewhere along the winding country road, everything went wrong. The screech of tires, the shatter of glass, and then a silence deeper than any he had ever known. *When Whiskers finally opened his eyes, the world was upside down and empty.* The doors hung open, and the rain poured in. He called out for Emma, for little Tommy, for anyone at all. *Only the wind answered him.*

For days, the cat refused to leave the crash site. He waited by the roadside, certain his family would come back for him. Kind strangers left food and water, but he would not budge. *He was waiting for the sound of Tommy's laughter, the smell of Mrs. Morrison's cooking, the familiar rumble of that old blue car.* None of it ever came. On the ninth day, a rescue worker named Dana found him shivering beneath the wrecked vehicle. She wrapped him in a warm blanket and whispered, *You're safe now, little one.*

Whiskers spent the following months at the shelter, withdrawn and silent. He would not play with toys, would not chase the feather wands the volunteers dangled for him. He simply sat in the corner of his enclosure, staring at the wall. *Grief, it seemed, was not a burden carried only by humans.* The volunteers began to worry that he would never recover.

Then one afternoon, a quiet girl named Lily visited the shelter with her grandmother. Lily had recently lost her own parents in a house fire and had moved in with her grandmother across town. She walked slowly past the row of cages, her eyes downcast, until she stopped in front of Whiskers. *Something in his lonely green eyes mirrored the ache in her own heart.* She pressed her small fingers against the glass, and for the first time in months, Whiskers moved. He approached the barrier and placed his paw exactly where her hand rested. *It was as if two broken souls had finally recognized each other.*

Lily's grandmother adopted him that very day. In the new apartment, Whiskers was cautious at first. He hid under the bed, refusing to eat, refusing even the warmest blankets. But Lily understood. *She did not rush him, because she knew what it meant to lose everything overnight.* Instead, she sat on the floor beside the bed every evening, reading stories aloud in a soft voice. Slowly, Whiskers began to inch closer. First a paw, then a head, then finally his entire trembling body. *By the second week, he was sleeping curled against her side.*

Healing did not happen all at once. There were still nights when Whiskers startled awake, searching for faces that would never return. There were moments when Lily cried quietly, and the cat would climb onto her chest and purr until her tears subsided. *They were learning, together, that love does not end when a family is gone.* It simply finds a new place to live.

One year later, Whiskers sat on the windowsill of the apartment, watching the autumn leaves fall. Lily was doing homework at the kitchen table, occasionally glancing over with a smile. Her grandmother was baking bread, filling the home with a scent that reminded him, gently, of another kitchen long ago. *The ache never fully disappeared, but it had softened into something he could carry.* Whiskers closed his eyes and purred. *He had lost one family, but somehow, against all odds, he had found another.* And this time, he promised himself, he would never let go.

Writing is a skill that anyone can develop with dedication and the right approach. Whether you're crafting emails, essays, or creative stories, becoming a better writer opens doors in both your personal and professional life. In this post, we'll explore practical strategies to elevate your craft.

***

## Practice Daily

The single most important habit for improving your writing is consistency. You must PRACTICE regularly, even if it's just for fifteen minutes a day. ***

Here are three essential techniques that will make an immediate difference:

* **Read widely and often.** Great writers are great readers. Exposing yourself to different genres, styles, and authors expands your vocabulary and teaches you what works on the page.

***

## Final Thoughts

Becoming a skilled writer doesn't happen overnight, but the journey is incredibly rewarding. Every expert was once a beginner, and progress comes from showing up consistently. # The Time Capsule

The house was smaller than Marianne remembered, the way all childhood houses are when you return to them as an adult. Her aunt's porch sagged in the middle now, and the oak tree her grandfather planted had grown so wide its branches pressed against the shingles.

She had driven four hours to be here, away from her mortgage and her half-empty refrigerator and the job she'd stopped calling a career. In the car, she'd rehearsed answers to the questions adults ask each other: *How's work? Are you seeing anyone? Isn't it crazy how time flies?*

When she arrived, the cousins were already there.

That was the strange thing — at thirty-eight, they were still called cousins, though the word had changed shape. As children, cousins meant armies and alliances, someone to blame when the vase broke, bare feet in the sprinkler, secrets traded under blanket forts. Now cousins meant people who knew your maiden name and your worst haircut and loved you anyway, but whom you saw perhaps twice a year, in brief intervals filled with potato salad.

Danny had gone gray at the temples. He sold insurance in Columbus and had a daughter exactly the age Marianne had been the summer they buried the time capsule. Sophie was on her second marriage and her first garden. Little Ray — who had never been little, who once pushed Marianne off the garage roof onto a mattress and called it science — was quiet now, holding a beer he didn't drink, recently divorced.

They stood around the grill, and it took an hour of small talk before someone finally said it:

"Remember the time capsule?"

They found the spot easily, as if their feet had never forgotten the coordinates. The jar was rusted, the notebook inside swollen with damp, the handwriting of nine-year-olds looping and certain. *In ten years we will be rich and famous,* Danny had written. *We will live in the same neighborhood forever.*

They laughed until Marianne's eyes stung, and she realized she wasn't laughing at the predictions. She was laughing because they had all made it here at all — scattered across four states, carrying divorces and diagnoses and dead parents, and still, when someone said *dig*, they dropped to their knees in the dirt like it was nothing.

Later, after the burgers and the small ceremonies of adult conversation, she found herself on the porch with Danny's daughter, seven years old, who asked if Marianne had any kids.

"No," she said. "Just a cat."

"Oh." The girl considered this. "Do you like being a grown-up?"

Marianne looked out at the yard — at Danny teaching his daughter to throw a spiral, at Sophie photographing the light through the oak, at Ray finally laughing at something.

"Most days," she said. "Today especially."

Because here was the thing about adulthood no one warned you about: it didn't take childhood away. It just filed it somewhere deep, and every few years, if you were lucky, someone handed you a shovel and said, *dig here.*

<<A House That Is Not a House>>

Not every house has walls. Not every house keeps out the rain, holds a family, or smells of Sunday dinner. Some houses are built entirely out of words, tradition, and the occasional raised voice. The riddle below describes the strangest house of all — one you may have seen on the news, walked past in a capital city, or even voted for without ever stepping inside. Every clue is honest, even when it sounds impossible. Read slowly, and see if you can move in before the answer does.

**The Riddle**

I'm a house with no rooms, and I open no door,
No kitchen, no hallway, no attic, no floor.
I've no roof for the rain, no window for sun,
Yet elections decide who will sit when they're won.

I keep a Speaker, though I have not a mouth;
My members address me from North and from South.
My floor's where they gather to argue and plead,
And I pass all my bills — no money I need.

My whips never crack, though my members obey;
My clerks write the record of all I say.
Three readings I get, though I've never a spine —
No pages, no chapters, no cover, no sign.

I'm labeled "the lower," or "the upper" with pride,
Though I've no stairs at all and no supper inside.
My divisions are votes, my recess is a rest,
My sessions run long, and my quorum's the test.

So here is my riddle, my puzzle, my art:
What house holds no family, no hearth, no heart?
I pass things all day, yet I stand in one place;
Name me, dear solver, with a smile on your face.

**The Answer**

The answer is a **legislative house** — the House of Representatives, the House of Commons, the House of Lords, or any parliamentary "house" in a congress or parliament.

**Explanation of the clues:**

- *A house with no rooms:* A legislative house is an institution — a body of people bound by rules and ritual — not a building with walls and windows.
- *A Speaker with no mouth:* The presiding officer of many such houses is literally titled the Speaker, as in "Speaker of the House."
- *My members and my floor:* Members of Parliament or Congress debate "on the floor" — meaning they've been recognized to speak, not that they're standing on floorboards.
- *Passing bills:* The bills a house passes are proposed laws, never currency, so the house never owes a cent.
- *Whips, clerks, and three readings:* Party whips enforce voting discipline, clerks keep the official record, and every bill is ceremonially read a first, second, and third time — though the house itself has no spine, pages, or cover.
- *Upper and lower:* Bicameral legislatures have "upper" and "lower" houses despite containing neither stairs nor basements.
- *Divisions, safe seats, recess, quorum:* In Westminster tradition, a "division" is a formal vote; a "safe seat" is one a party is expected to keep; a "recess" is a break in session; and a "quorum" is the minimum number of members required to do business.
- *I pass things all day, yet I stand in one place:* Bills pass; the house stands.

**Bonus:** This house has cousins. A full house in poker holds no rooms but is built from cards; a house of cards collapses with a single breath; and house music can fill a room all night while never collecting rent. English is full of houses with no address.

# <<Dreamweight>>

**Genre:** Neo-noir action / sci-fi drama
**Logline:** A retired boxer who can no longer dream enters an underground fighting league that exists inside shared dreams — where every fighter has a superpower born of their subconscious, and losing badly means losing pieces of your mind.

---

## ACT I — The Blank Nights

Elias "Eli" Ward was a middleweight contender until one punch ended his career and left his younger brother, Sam, in a coma. Ten years later, Eli works nights as a dream technician, guiding clients through lucid sleep with the Somnus rig. He's good at the job because he's the ideal subject — since the accident, Eli hasn't dreamed at all. His nights are blank tape.

One evening he catches an intruder in a client's dream: a scout for the **Nocturne League**, an underground fight circuit held inside a shared dream. In the League, skill and subconscious become one — fighters manifest powers drawn from who they truly are. A debt collector who slows time. A grieving mother whose skin turns to storm. A killer named **Vesper** who fights you with your own fears. Nobody bleeds in the real world — but fighters who lose badly come back hollowed out, missing memories. Some don't come back at all.

The scout recognizes Eli and tells him what he's waited a decade to hear: Sam's coma isn't medical. His mind is being held deep in the League's territory, where its founder — a figure called the **Somnologue** — keeps the minds she harvests like candles.

## ACT II — The Circuit

Eli enters the League. The first time someone lands a clean punch, his power wakes up: **kinetic echo** — every blow he takes, he keeps. Pain becomes weight behind his own hands. A life built on absorbing hits, made literal.

Fight by fight — a cathedral built from his childhood memories, a train that never arrives, the frozen second of the car crash he's never once revisited — Eli climbs the bracket. The bouts are brutal, bare-knuckle, staged in dreams that fight back. And as he wins, the blank nights start filling in. He dreams again, and what returns isn't pretty: the sound of that punch, guilt, Sam's voice in a hospital room where nobody said anything out loud.

Then the midpoint reveal: the Somnologue is not a dreamer. She is a *dream* — an old nightmare that learned to persist by feeding on sleeping minds. The League is her trough. And Sam wasn't random. Years ago, Sam found her first and fought to shut the door she was crawling through. That's why Eli's nights went dark — his brother sealed them to keep her out.

## ACT III — The Last Round

To reach Sam, Eli must win the championship. His opponent: the League's undefeated champion — Sam's own dream-self, puppeted from the inside, wearing his brother's face and throwing his brother's perfect right hand.

The fight is the film's centerpiece: two brothers in a dreamscape that keeps trying to become their childhood home, Eli refusing to swing back until he realizes the only winning move isn't technique. He stands in the pocket and takes everything his brother has — and with his echo burning, says the words that break the grip: *"You can stop. I've got you now."*

The dream-Sam lets go. The Somnologue comes for Eli herself. Her power is simple: she offers painless, guiltless blankness — and takes the mind that accepts. Against her, Eli's echo becomes a trapdoor. She tries to drink him and instead drinks ten years of absorbed pain, guilt, and love at full weight. He pours everything into one final punch — not to defeat her, but to knock the dream's floor out from under them both, and to carry Sam while it falls.

## Epilogue

In a hospital room, monitors that have read the same for a decade suddenly shift. Sam's fingers curl. Eli is asleep in the chair beside him — *actually* asleep — dreaming of the ocean.

In the dream, there's a door. It's locked. And from the other side, something scratches.
